message.content:
**Earliest non‑Christian historical reference to Jesus Christ**

| Source | Date (approx.) | Passage & Context | Why it matters |
|--------|----------------|-------------------|----------------|
| **Flavius Josephus – *Antiquities of the Jews* (Book 18, Chapter 3)** | 93–94 CE | “Now there was about this time Jesus, a wise man, if it be lawful to call him a man… He was crucified by Pontius Pilate.” | Josephus was a first‑century Jewish historian writing for a Roman audience. His mention of “Jesus” is widely accepted by scholars as a genuine reference, though the passage has been subject to later Christian interpolation. It is the earliest surviving independent testimony that Jesus existed and was executed under Pontius Pilate. |
| **Tacitus – *Annals* (Book 15, Chapter 44)** | 116 CE | “The emperor Tiberius, after the death of Claudius, had Nero condemned to death the Christians, who were called by the name of Christ.” | Tacitus, a Roman senator and historian, confirms that Christians were persecuted under Nero and that “Christ” was the name of their founder. It corroborates the New Testament account of Jesus’ crucifixion. |
| **Pliny the Younger – *Letters* (Letter 10.96)** | 112 CE | “The Christians worship Christ as a god.” | Pliny’s letter to Emperor Trajan shows that by the early 2nd century Christians were already venerating Christ as a divine figure. |
| **Babylonian Talmud – *Sanhedrin* 43a** | 3rd–5th century CE | “Jesus was hanged on the eve of Passover.” | A Jewish rabbinic text that records the crucifixion of Jesus, indicating that his execution was known among Jewish circles. |

### Bottom line
The **earliest surviving independent historical record** that mentions Jesus Christ is **Josephus’ *Antiquities* (c. 93–94 CE)**. Subsequent Roman historians (Tacitus, Pliny) and Jewish rabbinic texts also refer to him, but they come later. These references are crucial because they provide non‑Christian confirmation that Jesus existed, was crucified under Pontius Pilate, and that early Christians worshipped him as a divine figure.
